review:
I have played this game since the Closed Beta Testing, second week after first beta access. This game has gone through leaps and bounds since then, now over a year ago.  The Dev team has absolutely put in a lot of work, and it shows from the literal difference I have seen patch after patch. The latest patch, the June 2018 Patch, balanced champion health across the board with Light, Medium, and Heavy champs, respectively, along with some improvements to other aspects of the game. I expect a lot more to change and my recommendation is to pick this game up while it is free. This game is also recommended if you like fast paced and skill based shooters.

While the game is still technically Early Access, expect it to be different from the final release.

1. Its an arena shooter, expect you will be less than average the first time you pick it up, especially if you're new to arena fps.
2. Play the game, it is the only way to learn.
3. Check out FrothyOmen's Youtube tutorials on Champions.
4. Join the Quake Discord for additional help from community.
5. After about a month of playing, you will absolutley know if this is the game for you.

Bonuses: Every season the maps are udpated with seasonal textures, and vanity items, along with player icons and backgrounds. (santa hats, bunny ears, Spring textures, Snow textures)

Note: Most negative reviews of this game are blown out of proportion and are done by people with very few actual gameplay hours in this early access title.

[b]Would I prefer that they cut out all the champion BS and made every character play the same?[/b]
[list][*]Yes. Absolutely.[/*][/list]
[b]Is this still fun despite the differences in abilities, hit boxes, health, and armor between champions? [/b]
[list][*]Yes.[/*][/list]
[b]Can you find a game in any other arena shooter?[/b]
[list][*]Possibly in Quake Live but it's an extremely small community. As of October 2019 Quake Live was averaging 255 players online vs Quake Champion's average of 519 players. Unreal Tournament is dead. Toxikk is dead. Reflex Arena is dead.[/*][/list]
[b]Have id and Bethesda abandoned this game?[/b]
[list][*]Yes.[/*][/list]
[b]Is the death of this genre deeply depressing to me?[/b]
[list][*]YES.[/*][/list]

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
For me, QC feels decidedly like a Quake game.

Now, what's important to note here is that, while the game does introduce light Hero-Shooter elements, none of these profoundly impact the gameplay itself. You won't, for example, find that one Champion inherently trumps another, or that one ability is far stronger than what you could have accomplished just with regular weapons.
In other words, I haven't felt as if I lost an engagement because of my or my opponents choice of Champion, nor that I suffered an unavoidable death simply due to an ability being used.

Some will argue that there is still less "Quake about it" due to these minor inclusions, and which side you agree with, will likely depend on whether or not you expect a new installment of the franchise, or a remastering of a previous installment. 

If the former, it'll feel like Quake - a new Quake game.
If the latter, it won't quite be Quake - close, but no provebial cigar.

And the obvious retort here is that, if you belong to the latter, then there's still Quake Live as a valid alternative.

For me, it still feels as fast as the good old days, and with as much potential for the high skill-ceiling as in old iterations - but again, some will disagree.

[b]Balance:[/b]
I'm actually amazed at how well everything is balanced at this point. No Champion feels vastly superior or inferior to others, but instead cater to certain playstyles (via their mobility-centered passives; some mimicking older Quake games, some mimicking UT, and so on).

It can be frustrating to face certain Champions from time to time, but only if you let yourself get convinced that it had more to do with their choice of Champion, than that players own level of skill - and personally, I've only ever seen it be a case of the latter, never the former.

In addition to that, the Devs are monitoring their data on the matter closely - as was reported in a recent AUA Stream - and they have said as much as they would rather elevate other champions, than nerf one champion, if push comes to shove. For the time being, however, the data shows very little imbalance - some Champions may be picked more often than others in certain modes, but no single Champion outperforms another substantially.

Personally, I no longer even consider Champion "power" when picking mine for a match, there's no point - it's that level of balanced, I find.

[b]Anti-cheat:[/b]
While not implemented just yet, I haven't personally encountered any Cheaters in my time in the game (joined in CBT2). They've been gathering data on the ones that have been found, however, and restructured the base code to combat it directly, while also collaborating with another team to specfically implement an active anti-cheat, which we should see in the coming months.

[b]Monetization:[/b]
While prices on cosmetics can be steep, they are also easily obtainable just by playing the game.
You roughly get 1 Backpack (common loot-box with 1 item) every 2 - 3 matches; costs 2000 in-game currency, and you earn about 800-1000 per match. And you also have Daily Challenges which can net you between 4500 - 9000 Favour total, per day.
You get 1 Chest (uncommon loot-box with 2 items) each level, and you level up roughly every 7 - 12 matches.
You get 1 Reliquary (rare loot-box with 3 items) every 5 levels.

Additionally, while this will only go into affect once QC exits Early Access, if you start a free account, you start only with Ranger, but you can rent any Champion for 24 hours for 5000 Favour.
Furthermore, there is a relatively good chance that a Champion will drop permanently from Reliquaries, and even a very low chance they will drop from Backpacks. 
However, during EA, the entry-fee will automatically net you all current and future Champions.

For reference, while anecdotal, I personally have earned a total of about 10 Champions over the course of the Beta, out of a total of about 15 Reliquaries (i.e. by level 75).

[b]Community:[/b]
In general, a very welcoming and open community. The amount of sober discussions far outweigh the number of toxic ones, and contrary to the vast majority of communities I've anticipated in in the past - with one notable exception (you know who you are <3) - people are more likely to listen to well-formulated and founded counter-arguments, rather than stubbornly insist on their initial thoughts and feelings on the matter, which again makes for a very welcoming feel.

Furthermore, it's one of the most helpful communities I've been a part of; in the vast majority of cases, new players seeking advice are given constructive and well thought out feedback, and in no way ridiculed, whether they do this on the official forums or by posting a YouTube video or what not.

All in all, I have mostly very positive things to say about the community. There are, of course, some bad seeds now and again, but they're only an ignore function away, and other people will often either ignore them and keep playing (if in-game), or marvel at their poor attempts at smack-talk.

[b]Development:[/b]
First and foremost, the positives: Devs seem aware of the issues at hand, they've done a decent job of both polishing the core mechanics and functionality, while also releasing new content, and they've been relatively open about things when they finally open up.

But that's generally where the down-side comes into play: They aren't open very often. Most of the time, a poor CM is tasked with relaying what info the Devs deem necessary, so players often feel left out, especially if an urgent issue has arisen. Likewise, they very, very rarely respond on forums, or even post updates or roadmaps, but instead rely heavily on Discord to communicate with their playerbase, meaning information could (and arguably has) gotten lost easily, since no kind player was around to copy/paste that needed information onto the forums.

Granted, they are currently in the final stages of a prize tournament - which one could question the wisdom of having at this point - so they are obviously very busy. 
They have stated, however, that they want to increase the level of community outreach in the future, so time will tell whether that will happen or not.

[b]Performance:[/b]
It's a bit hit-and-miss for some. There are still some hit-reg and netcode issues, but for most (assumption) they've improved since the EA patch - for most, they've improved since early Beta.
There are, of course, exceptions to this, but from what I can gather, it is as much a server-related issue as anything, so it may just be teething issues as they also upgrade servers to handle the new influx of players, but now I'm speculating.

There is one persistent memory leak that hasn't quite been fixed yet, but it only comes into player after 4-5 matches, and is quickly remedied by relaunching the client.


[b]All in all:[/b]
- A good base for a new, fresh installment of Quake, but only if you are willing to let go of the notion that it should be a remastered Quake 1/2/3/4/Live. 
- Balance is excellent, the only time you'll feel as if you lost due to your choice of Champion, is if you convince yourself of as much.
- Cheating is a non-issue, I'd say - but if you are new, skilled players can easily give the impression that they are cheating - but it is something the Devs take very seriously, and from all accounts, they're just about ready to roll out the proverbial big guns.
- Monetization is a bit steep at the moment, but there are plenty of ways to earn it by simply playing.
- Community is excellent, very open and welcoming, and eager to help new players while also being respectful towards each other - both on official forums and other avenues - but there are obviously bad seeds occasionally, but not very often.
- Development is competent but opaque for the moment being, but Developers have stated they are looking to become more transparent in the future. 
- Performance is hit-and-miss for some, but overall has improved since earlier versions.

As a long-time fan of the Quake series, having spent hundreds of hours in previous versions, I eagerly tried out Quake Champions. However, I must admit that I wasn't entirely thrilled with the new iteration. My sentiments seem to align with other reviews expressing similar concerns.

In my opinion, introducing abilities to Quake dilutes the franchise's core focus on skill. Quake's success has been built on mastering aim, timing, and movement rather than relying on special abilities. The game has a rich history, with legendary frag movies that many of us fondly remember watching at LAN parties.

That said, I understand the need for the Quake series to evolve and adapt to modern gaming trends. Quake Champions is a commendable attempt at innovation, but it hasn't quite hit the mark yet. The gameplay feels less polished than it should be, with room for improvements to deliver a more satisfying experience.

In conclusion, Quake Champions offers a nostalgic trip down memory lane for fans of the series, but it also presents a somewhat divisive take on the classic game. It's a step forward in terms of development, but some adjustments are needed to retain the essence of what made Quake an iconic game in the first place.

It might not be Q3A, but Quake Champions is a damn fine shooter, a great Quake game, and an incredible amount of fun. The Champion system is actually surprisingly well designed, pretty deep and doesn't hurt the core gameplay - the champions are all pretty balanced and the abilities add something new to the gameplay. Beyond that, QC is the best choice if you're an arena shooter fan - it is a modernized take on Quake, but it's still just as enthralling, rewarding and punishing as Quake 3 was two decades ago.

The game's still in Early Access, so some issues may be present and the content offering is still being built up, but overall my experience has been great so far. Definitely worth playing.

In all, it's still early access. Odds are they're going to want to get as much money as they can from this. But for now I do recommend it and I'll just be hopeful that actually put some thought and care into this. As things go along I'll update the review.

This is Quake brought to a new era! Quake Champions is simply the fastest, most rewarding and fun FPS available. You can dabble in other games, but at the end of the day once you've completed the single player campaign in a day or two or even spent a while in the multiplayer, Quake is the one game you keep returning to. Nothing beats careering around the map, boosting yourself along or up in the air by throwing a rocket under your own feet or against a wall, flipping around and taking out an opponent with a well-placed rail, or frying them with your lightning gun if they're still close enough.

Before I carry on, I'd just like to make it very clear that this game is not pay to win, it is entirely skill based, the only changes to functionality in gameplay are your champion picks and they can all be earned for free. Absolutely everything else in the game is cosmetic only, even if it jokes about a breastplate attachment giving more armour, it doesn't, it's cosmetic.

This game is fun for new players fighting to get a few frags, or competing with their peers, and still amazing at even the absolute highest levels of skill able to compete in tournaments for thousands of dollar prizes. The graphics are modern, colourful and vibrant and the new gibs/gore system recently released is gory enough to satisfy all and one of the most versatile in any FPS.

There are negative reviews from old school Quake players that simply wanted new graphics on their old game, they cannot accept the truth that that simply [b]would not work[/b] this decade. Reflex Arena is basically exactly this, and has fewer than one hundred concurrent players despite being a fantastic and well produced game. QC brings a range of different characters to the game as was originally planned for Quake 3 Arena and successfully balances them in a game where they all have a strong chance of winning in the right hands.

Don’t be put off by only having Ranger to start as a free to play player, Ranger is absolutely one of the best champions in the game, with his very reduced self-damage you can rocket jump around more freely, and his dire orb teleportation and damage is very powerful indeed.

Quake Champions brings in the best of previous Quake game's skills all into one, love the movement from CPMA (QuakeLive PQL) then try Anarki or Sorlag, love the crouch sliding from Quake 4? Then try Slash. Love traditional Quake 2, 3, Quake Live movement (vq3)? Then most of the other characters are for you. There's even the DOOM Slayer for those that struggle with strafe jumping, Clutch with a little bit of double tap dodge and Scalebearer if you… like trains ;o)
If you’re completely new to Quake then seeking some movement guides for the champions you like the look of is definitely the way to go (see links below) until such guides are incorporated into the game itself, as is planned. Learning at least a little of the movement systems available really opens up the possibilities in the game and they’re the first steps to the largest gains.

Not all characters will be for everyone as their varying sizes and movement abilities make them all very different to play, but when you find one or two that suit your style, the experience is like no other, no other game gives the same satisfaction with its frags, both from the visuals and the feeling of achievement.

The pace is exhilarating, and the casual game modes can be quite hectic especially on the few smaller maps, but stealing a few frags and working your way through the daily and rune challenges can still be done at any level, the larger more open maps offer some more laid back stealthy play, and if that’s your main interest then Duel is perhaps best suited for you as it gives the freedom to really play your own way without having to worry about escaping from more than your single opponent.

Beyond the solo modes, ranked 2v2 is a very popular and highly competetive duo mode to play with a friend, voice coms highly reccomended, the same is true for Team Deathmatch which is 4v4, but that is an unranked mode. Capture the Flag (CTF) and Clan Arena are also planned for the future.

All in, the best multiplayer FPS available.

Quake Champions is an interesting game, and people seem to be divided on it. Most complaints have to do with Performance, netcode, and loot boxes. Performance is iffy, it seems to vary system to system, patch to patch. For me personally i've always been able to get over 110fps, which isn't the 144 i want but it's acceptable. 

I haven't experienced too many bad netcode issues, occasionally I'll die behind a corner but it's rare enough. Client side hit detection is fine with me, it would be near impossible to play with anyone over 40 ping otherwise. I agree it could be slightly better but I've never experienced a game where I thought I would have won if hit detection was better. 

Loot boxes are another thing, the game is plenty generous with the lowest tier box and the second tier chests are decently available, you'll be getting a chest or two a day due to leveling and Rune challenges. The one paid lootbox in the game is trash however and for the equivalent of $4 real world dollars is kind of an insult, it says it drops high quality gear but can drop greys and greens as often as it drops purps and golds. It's important to remember that loot boxes are ENTIRELY COSMETIC and have no gameplay effect. I'm not happy with how many lower quality items there are that take up the loot pool and with high tier boxes but it's not a dealbreaker for me.

I've also heard that the game has some cheaters, which I don't doubt is true but I can't say I've ran into a person I can 100% be sure is cheating. However I've been accused of cheating multiple times, even in highish ELOs so I think players calling cheats may be biased.

The most important part of a quake game is the gameplay and I've been very satisfied with it. Aside from one or two "ultimate" abilities the game seems to be balanced very well, all the weapons feel like they should and are satisfying to use and to combo. There are a few characters with different movement styles that spice up the game if you want to take the time to learn them as well as normal Quake movement which is very fun to master in itself. I've never really lost a game where I felt that I was better than an opponent but they won due to character choice except maybe with the new Death Knight character but I'm confident he'll recieve a rework. The game is definitely brutal for new players and if you have no prior experience with arena shooters you're going to get your ass handed to you for a while, but thankfully matchmaking seems to have been improved and during the day there's a big enough pool of players where your games will be relatively balanced. A larger playerbase would improve this however. If you're picking up a Quake game or an Arena shooter game for the first time you're going to have to be patient and learn but if you do you'll be rewarded with dopamine rush after dopamine rush of getting cooler and cooler kills that once seemed like a pipe dream.

In conclusion, Quake Champions has issues, and despite a few changes that make it more friendly to newcomers is still a very hard game to pick up. But if you take the time to improve and don't get too frustrated you will find it an extremely rewarding test of FPS abilities. If you are interested in a fragfest game with an infinite skill ceiling and can grind for personal improvement I think it's defintely worth getting, especially if you can pick it up for free and if you like playing as the starting champ, Ranger, then the whole champions pack may be worth buying. I recommend this game with the caveat that if you haven't had prior arena shooter experience it might still be too intimidating of a climb even if it is the most newcomer friendly version of Quake.

After playing Quake 1's multiplayer, Q3 Live and then going back to Quake Champions after 9 years of not playing it, QC has shockingly NOT improved at all.

To start this review the game has great character designs, they all come from different dimensions and uniquely stand out from each other, each character also has unique first person animations and it's really nice attention to detail, however the roster falls a little short and maybe ID should reintroduce older Quake characters like Crash or Bones for nostalgia value. 

Their abilities on the other hand do not fit into Quake's core gameplay loop at all your ability or "ultimate" is essentially a free win button, ID should add an option to matchmaking to play with abilities enabled or not. As for the gameplay itself excluding the ultimates I guess it's still a Quake game, although slower with much less gamemodes than Quake 3 Live, they should do some touch up's on the heads up display and make sounds like footsteps louder so players can tell where enemies are coming from.

Second, customisation, it's really bad in this game, sure there are a few favourites people will have for classic gun models but I really wish Quake Champions had the level of customisation DooM 2016's multiplayer had, changing individual colors and the wear and tear of weapons and armor was really sick and being able to actually earn them through gameplay instead of an in-game cash shop was much more rewarding, ID should add it into this game with some basic colors to work with as a starter and expand on the shader system.

Quake Champions with custom maps and game modes would MASSIVELY increase this game's appeal and longevity, not only that but it would also prevent any pressure on ID from having to make another multiplayer component for any future Quake game should they ever decide to make a 5th one or a remake, it would be a balanced ecosystem for singleplayer and multiplayer Quake fans. 

My conclusion? The game needs a 2.0 overhaul for it's 10th anniversary, bring back modding for custom content, overhaul systems like the ultimates and rework customisation in the game. Been playing since Quake 3 and Quake Champions is both a step in the right and wrong directions. TL;DR at the bottom.

[u]The Good:[/u]
[list]
[*]Quake Champions brings the classic hardcore arena shooter into the 21st century with buttery smooth controls, and a much appreciated face lift in the graphics department. ID and Saber did a great job developing this title for a modern audience and took a lot of time and care to make sure it could compete in the market. I was afraid they would go overboard and make the arenas to dark to effectively see the enemy, but that's not the case at all.

[*]Gun play is rewarding and the learning curve to becoming a better player is still there. This really shows up specifically when using the rail gun. The zoom feature helps out with aiming and easees the pressure on players having to squint or lean in to their screen when lining up a shot form afar. It has become a bit easier to use, but still takes time to learn how to hit flick shots and gaining confidence in your aim. You'll notice improvement with each game whether you win or loose and that is one of the addictive qualities of these titles.

[*]Movement is a lot easier and more accessible now too. Strafe jumping feels a lot better and somehow more effortless in this iteration than previous titles. Rocket jumping/propelling is still the same along with various other methods of getting extra boost such as using the nail gun or tri-bolt in lieu of rockets. Certain heroes also add to the fun of moving around at stupid speeds.

[*]Map design is super important to quake as there needs to be a certain amount of verticality and fluidity when getting around the map. Controlling major items is a top priority so these maps have to allow a person who's in control to freely fly through the map seeking their opponent, but also give the out of control player enough space to sneak around in while providing openings to regain control themselves. There are only a handful of maps, some are new some are classic staples, and you'll become familiar with them extremely fast.

[*]The Introduction of casual/fun arcade game types such as instagib and unholy trinity are great for warming up or just messing around. The inclusion of a ranked system was also a much needed feature when grinding out matches, and just going up against competent players.

[*]It's now free to play! I bought into the game when it was on sale for $5, and after seeing what they were doing with the title it felt like even that was a bit much.

[/list]

[u]The Bad:[/u]
[list]
[*]Hero Shooter.... They decided to turn quake... into a hero shooter.... What this means is that you now have meta lineups. There's always going to be 1-2 heroes that get picked no matter what and the rest get pushed to the wayside until the developers decide to change it up somehow. It's tiresome to stick to a meta not to mention boring unless drastic changes get made to how heroes and abilities work in a timely manner. It feels like a decision that was made because Overwatch. 

It can really ruin the game at times when you've gotten your enemy down to railable health, but they're playing Galena so they just retreat to whatever little corner they've stacked three totems in and get themselves up to 175 HP leaving you to run the map. Before the current patch this review was written on, I remember ranger was basically able to tele frag you just by shoving his orb into your chest as soon as you showed up. It just doesn't fit Quake where the gun play and skills it takes to win are the funnest part about playing the game. Now I gotta bait out Clutch's dumb shield and then somehow deal with his ridiculous amount of stack. The various amounts of health and shield are also quite annoying and sometimes lopsided.

[*]Three strikes you're out system. You each get three heroes and the first person to three frags wins the round. I both like and hate this type of system. I like that it can greatly reduce match time depending on who you go up against. If you just wipe the floor with them then you're not going to be stuck for a long drawn out match, and if you're equally competent then you'll have a lot of fun the whole time trading blows.

I hate the sudden death overtime as I favored the 10 minutes matches where if you've tied the score you get an extra  2 minutes to win it. It's not the worst thing to happen, but it can also lead to matches where you'll have a great counter pick against your opponents hero, but because you slipped up a bit or they nailed an insane shot, you quickly get into a position where you now have the worst counter pick and your opponent just steam rolls you to victory.

[*]Daily Challenges, Battlepass, and the economy:

It's all a mess that I really don't want to spend time on because this review is already long enough as is. you get 3 daily challenges, super easy to complete in the first match you play. They don't give a lot of shards or whatever, and you'll have to wait a whole day for 3 challenges to refresh.

The new battlepass/weekly rewards change helps that slightly, but if you don't buy into the battlepass for whatever price their asking then you're missing out on more opportunities for skins, shards, and platinum currencies as you gain XP. Is it better than lootboxes? Hell no. It's pure garbage and now takes away more chances for a F2P person to get new/interesting skins.

Also you can still buy lootboxes? How many greedy things can we shove into this bad boy?

The economy sucks just like every other F2P game that offers a free and premium version. 

[/list]

[u]The Ugly:[/u]
[list]
[*][b][u]MICRO-TRANSACTIONS!!!![/u][/b]

You'll get two freebie characters to start with, ranger and scalebearer, then if you want to do ranked you're stuck with whoever they make free to play at the time. I grinded to unlock slash before they brought the price requirement down and it's still a chore. I also got lucky that they hosted a community event where everyone playing at the time got Athena for free when we hit a certain milestone. I doubt they'll be giving away a free character like that again as the community really stepped up and made short work of the challenge given. Maybe they will, but increase the target to reach some ungodly number.

The prices are ridiculous and you'll need to spend money or grind a stupid amount of time away to unlock all the  characters. I paid $5 dollars to get into the game and now I have to spend $20 to unlock just the characters. On top of that you'll spend $5-$10 on a single skin. Want to make grinding less of a chore? Purchase and XP booster for $2. Want to increase the loot you get with the XP booster, or get more weekly challenges? Purchase a Battlepass for $10.

Do you want to change your nickname because you messed up a letter or just want to change it up? 1500 platinum/$15. You have to pay them to change your in-game name, and it's a stupidly high amount to do so. A basic skin shader costs 200 platinum.

Also, lootboxes are still in the game, but instead of getting them for playing and rolling the dice on what you get they're a premium feature now. You can only buy a premium lootbox and still roll the dice "with at least one item of legendary quality" in each one. 400 platinum/$5 a pop.

You can't grind enough in the game without spending money to afford anything!

[/list]

To start off this review, I gotta say that this is the first Quake game I have played. And it made me want to get all the other Quake games and play through them.  I love this game and it's a blast to play with non-stop action. But I can't recommend Quake Champions in its current state to everyone. When the devs fix those two main problems then the game will be a lot easier to recommend. 

The gameplay itself is incredible, netcode issues aside, I never seem to have a dull moment when I play this game besides waiting in the lobby for the next game to start (which can take several minutes). I would end up getting destroyed when I first played the game but that didn't stop me. I wanted to get better at it. I played a bit and got better at strafe jumping, found out which characters I enjoy playing as, and learned the weapon/health placements on the maps. I like the grind of Quake because there will always be someone that's better than you at something. You have to dedicate time to practicing your jumps and you need to know when you should use certain weapons over others. Yeah I did rage a lot, but I'm a lot better than when I first started playing. Now I usually come in first, second, or third in the game and I'm really enjoying it.

Now just because I really like this game doesn't mean everyone should go buy it right now. Once the game launches it will be F2P and you will have one champion to start out with and you will be able to unlock the other champions without paying. So unless you are a diehard arena shooter fan I would say wait until the F2P version comes out and try that out.

I don't think it's fair to say this is a free to play game. I think that's probably the biggest misconception about it. Don't get me wrong, you don't have to pay a cent to enjoy it. Rewards are abundant and things unlock swiftly.

The price I had to pay was time. It's one of those games that takes a long time to feel good. Like playing guitar, the beginning is slow, clunky, embarrassing and full of mistakes. Unlike learning to play guitar, you must do it together with others who are already good at it. Some are untouchable virtuoso's. Failure translates to being at the bottom of the match scoreboard. 

 [i]For a long time. 

And I wanted to learn enough to climb out on my own skill. [/i]

In short, it's a beautiful and difficult game with a lot to master. Being good at it makes you good at almost any shooter. It requires patience and dedication to become competent. It makes some concessions to current trends (free-to-play, microtransactions), but not enough to be annoying.

It's my favourite shooter at the moment. I recommend it because the matches go very fast, there's not much active focus done by the brain that can help. It's a game that's less about thinking and more about feeling. And I love how that is. To find the groove of the match, the dance and my place in it. It's a blast.

[i]And so it was that at the beginning, with poor aim and no map awareness I had to be able to find a way to contribute. Die less. Distract more. Assist more. Run faster. Don't hit walls. Don't back step outside the map. Negate power-ups. [/i]

Movement is tight and its mastery is crucial for good results. And so much fun! Each weapon has character, purpose and unique utility. I really love how I have a limited set of inputs (WSAD, jump, fire, weapon switch and ability), yet the game is incredibly deep in its mechanics (classic Quake). Playing the game does feel like practising an instrument, where I'm constantly trying to tighten my timings, to have my jump strafing that much more effective and controlled, my movement around the map more efficient and my control of power-ups more assertive.

[i]Slowly but surely I started to climb out of the bottom. Started to control certain fights. To anticipate certain moves. To have a more positive impact. Started to find a way. My way.[/i]

Game performance has been no issue. I get stable >100 fps at 1080p on a i5-7500 with a GTX 1050 Ti and 16 GB RAM, on custom settings. The game looks great and feels super responsive and smooth on 4 year old budget-ish hardware. There's a satisfaction in running something so nice and nicely without having to spend more money.

I love whizzing around the fantastic medieval horror sci-fi maps, taking in the cool little details that tie to the lore. Each champion is oozing with character and menace. There are some "funny" cosmetics that run against the overall theme of the game, but they're not too abundant and things move quickly it's hard for me to be bothered. The abilities add flavour, but I've never seen one deciding a TDM match. An engagement here and there, sure. They can be decisive in duels between evenly matched players, but then everything is decisive when it helps getting ahead. Another cool detail is how enemy champion size and speed influences weapon selection. Another bit of flavour and variety, so that engagements don't follow such a simple formula. It suits me well.

[i]With my ease with mechanics, my game knowledge prospered. I faithfully stuck with Galena. Who best to contribute at low levels, by healing the team? At least that. I would at least try to help my better team mates. And to reinforce the faith in my practice and my champion, I would celebrate when I saw a more advanced player absolutely dominate a match with Galena. The healer. The death dealer.[/i]

I'm a casual player who logs in, throws the match maker up, runs a few matches, logs out. The MTX don't bother me, being safely put away in a different menu. No prompts to go buy stuff other than the one running with the information of my daily challenges. I get enough unlocks by just playing the game, I'm happy with my champion and weapon cosmetic customisation options.

I've been able to get a match quickly at any time of day (Central European Time). There's enough people to always get a match, but I don't think there's enough people around for quirky stuff. This mess is what happens when you take one of the most iconic, competitive and perfected franchises in gaming history, combine it with a useless publisher, outsource development to an incompetent game studio and make Adam Pyle - who single handedly ruined Quake Live - the lead designer. This is the pinnacle of incompetence and bad development. It's so ridiculous, I can't even find the right words for it.

There's virtually no progress. If you look at the patches, which take between 4 and 8 weeks, 90% are balancing changes to weapons and champions, which is literally just changing a server variable and can't even remotely be considered development, with the remaining 10% being mostly additions to the in-game store. That's cheap cash-grab strategy at its finest. While I couldn't care less about the ridiculous loot system, the massive focus on it has no place in a beta or the early stages of EA. As with Quake Live, the community is being spat on - things that no one asked for are changed and what people want is ignored.

If you consider that most of the core game algorithms already existed from previous titles, the only thing they actually developed are the abilities (which are mostly broken or buggy) and the netcode. And boy is the netcode bad. This is without a doubt the worst netcode in FPS history. It's even worse than Doom 2016, which I didn't think was possible.

As for the gameplay: yes, it still feels like quake, but that's about it. Everthing else is anywhere from mediocre to bad. And no, it's not about the champions. While I, personally, don't like them, they don't necessarily overshadow the core gameplay. At least if they were implemented in a sensible way, which isn't the case either at the moment. Most of what made Quake great is gone. They removed or dumbed down so many of the franchise's time-proven features that you're left with a random, inconsistent pile of cow manure. On top of that, the few maps they provided so far are mediocre at best. They even managed to screw up Q3DM6, which, while heavily overplayed, was arguably one of the best maps ever created.

Being a Quaker for over 20 years now, I felt obliged to get this game, even though I was always sure it was going to be garbage, given who is in charge. So that's what you can expect to see when you buy the game - mostly Quake veterans that are putting up with it, because it's the closest thing to a new Quake they're going to get. The daily average has been around 300 with a daily peak of around 1000 for months now and it's not going to change. And don't give me that "it's still beta" crap. Anyone with the IQ of a loaf of bread should know how Steam works. Once it's available as Early Access, it's effectively released. Games that are dead during Early Access will stay dead. That's how it has always been and that's how it's always going to be.
